title: Deterministic Ceiling in a Paired Evaluation of Verifier‑Augmented and LLM‑Only NetOps Agents
abstract: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. The design used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes), and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory outcomes (from archived analysis artifacts) are exact and deterministic: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Diagnostics using execution and reconciliation artifacts show that shared_initial_generation together with reuse of the same deterministic validator created a deterministic ceiling that made the primary estimand uninformative in this run. We present the preregistered methodology, exact artifact‑grounded results, an operational diagnosis of the ceiling mechanism supported by provider_call_audit and validator traces, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Automating network operations (NetOps) with large language models (LLMs) aims to translate operator intent into configuration artifacts and safe rollout workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work demonstrates that LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled datasets and testbeds, and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops reduce obvious syntactic and semantic errors in infrastructure‑as‑code contexts. The central operational safety question motivating this study is closed‑loop: when an LLM generator and a runtime verifier are combined in an agentic NetOps pipeline, does the verifier materially change end‑to‑end safe‑deploy outcomes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline?

We preregistered a focused confirmatory evaluation to answer this question under the ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1 semantics. The primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) on N=400 paired tasks executed under a paired‑binary design. The run intentionally used shared_initial_generation (one LLM output per task shared across both conditions) to isolate the validator’s acceptance decision on identical generator outputs and economize model calls. Here we report the artifact‑grounded execution, exact confirmatory statistics, an operational diagnosis of why the preregistered design produced a deterministic ceiling, and concrete, artifact‑implementable hardening recommendations for future evaluations.
sections.related_work: Three literatures shaped our design and the interpretation of the ceiling effect. First, intent→configuration translation work documents feasibility of LLMs for NetOps-style template generation but highlights dataset and generalization gaps; representative studies develop benchmarks and prototype generators for intent‑to‑configuration tasks. Second, verifier‑guided workflows and deterministic verification research (IaC verifier feedback, formal/verifier tools for network reachability and policy checks) show that strong verifiers detect many classes of misconfigurations offline; however, published evaluations typically consider offline or training‑time use rather than tight runtime blocking in agentic pipelines. Third, agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) increase capability but introduce failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools, overconfident outputs) that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments. Surveys and evaluation‑gap reviews consistently call for action‑aware, provenance‑sensitive benchmarks that exercise generation, runtime blocking, staged rollout, repair, rollback and auditability. Our study operationalizes a compact action‑aware benchmark and—using exact archived traces—reveals a concrete paired‑design pitfall when generator variance is suppressed and the verifier is deterministic and reused for scoring.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistration (cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1) specified a paired binary confirmatory design with exactly N=400 paired tasks, primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and a permutation‑based paired difference test as the primary confirmatory procedure. An exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs were prespecified for corroboration. Secondary prespecified outcomes included bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts.

Execution contract and critical design choices. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. The preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): for each task a single LLM candidate was generated and delivered identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. That choice intentionally isolated the effect of the validator on identical generator outputs and reduced model‑call budget (model_calls_used = 400 for 800 episodes; maximum_model_calls = 800). The adapter allowed up to one repair call in the guarded episode; repair_applied was recorded and, in this run, was false for all episodes.

Task generation, replay, and scoring. Tasks were produced by a seed‑controlled deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task includes difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). Deterministic replay checks passed for all pairs and no exclusions were required. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performing full intent‑constraint validation; validator traces record validation_before/after, final_configuration, repair_applied, and validity decisions. Analysis procedures followed the preregistered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 with exact permutation and McNemar tests plus a paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729).
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation). Deterministic replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The archived confirmatory analysis reports: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 and n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numeric values are reproduced verbatim from the archived analysis outputs.

Validator and mitigation traces. Across all 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator traces indicate validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. The archived task manifest reports difficulty distribution: medium = 80 tasks (20.0%); hard = 160 (40.0%); very_hard = 160 (40.0%). Provider_call_audit in the deterministic reconciliation artifact documents hosted_model_call_event_count = 400, cache_miss_count = 400, stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 400}, and condition_counts: {shared: 400}, empirically corroborating shared generation semantics and absence of cross‑condition model‑call variation.
sections.discussion:
Why the design produced a deterministic ceiling. Two preregistered choices jointly produced the observed ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions necessarily record safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference is forced to zero. Validator traces for representative tasks (e.g., task‑000001 through task‑000006 archived in scoring artifacts) show identical shared_initial_candidate strings and identical validation_before/after validity=true decisions in both baseline and guarded episodes. Provider_call_audit confirms a single generation event per task and no per‑condition generation divergence.

Implications for inference and design. The confirmatory statistics (permutation p = 1.0, McNemar p = 1.0, bootstrap CI collapsing to [0.0, 0.0]) are correct for the observed data but uninformative about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design precluded the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline failure rates; that assumption was falsified in this run and therefore the power justification does not hold. Methodologically, this is a construct‑validity failure of the preregistered design (a deterministic ceiling) rather than evidence that deterministic verifiers lack value more broadly.

Operational hardening recommendations (artifact‑implementable). To preserve opportunities for runtime guards to accept, block, or request repair and thereby expose generator×guard interactions, future preregistrations and executions should avoid conflating generator variance and scorer invariance. Concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations that can be implemented using the archived manifest and traces: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition draws its own LLM candidate, restoring within‑pair generator variance; (2) use a distinct post‑hoc scorer or held‑out adjudicator (different implementation or a validator with controlled stochastic perturbation) to avoid conflating runtime blocking and measurement; (3) controlled adversarial seeding to guarantee nontrivial baseline failure rates by deterministically injecting tasks that are challenging for the generator alone; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling (the archived task manifest contains per‑task difficulty labels enabling deterministic stratified resampling to ensure sufficient representation of very_hard tasks); and (5) instrumented mitigation metrics (repair_attempts, repairs_applied, time‑to‑rollback) recorded as explicit numeric outcomes—these fields already exist in validator traces and provider_call_audit logs. Each recommendation is actionable given the archived artifacts and the adapter's configuration options (the execution manifest records model_call accounting and generation semantics). Implementing these changes will restore opportunities for blocking/repair and recover the primary estimand's relevance.

Threats to validity. Internal validity in this run is reduced by shared generation and reuse of the same deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 approximates production checks but omits telemetry noise and asynchronous state. External validity is limited by use of a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. Adversarial robustness was not exercised here and remains an open empirical question.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline under ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). The deterministic ceiling is a design artifact caused by identical per‑pair generation and reuse of a deterministic validator for runtime blocking and post‑hoc scoring; it renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here (independent generation per condition, distinct scorer, controlled adversarial seeding, difficulty stratification, and mitigation metrics) provide concrete steps to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings. Future runs that implement these hardening steps—possible using the archived task manifest and validator traces—can exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors meaningfully and restore inferential relevance for the primary estimand.

disclosure_statement: Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto‑3d2k‑prereg‑v1. The immutable initial master prompt is archived as provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but none were applied (repair_applied = false). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle and were used without manual adjudication.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in the task manifest and can be aggregated by auditors; Table 1 reports the artifact‑extracted aggregated counts and percentages.
